disclaimer: Informational, not medical advice. Check interactions and conditions with a clinician. Dose ranges are from the cited consensus documents. Anything tiered 'weak' or 'skip' is listed only so you know why it is not recommended.
gradingNote: Tiers follow the IOC 2018 consensus statement (good/strong evidence: caffeine, creatine, nitrate, bicarbonate, beta-alanine). Huberman Lab Wiki items are AI-generated summaries of podcast episodes and are graded by the underlying evidence, not by the podcast's claim.

A-strong.name: Creatine monohydrate
A-strong.dose: 3-5 g/day, any time; no loading needed
A-strong.goal: strength, power, lean mass, recovery; possible cognitive benefit
A-strong.notes: Most studied performance supplement. Choose plain monohydrate; expect 1-2 kg water weight gain.

A-strong.name: Caffeine
A-strong.dose: 3-6 mg/kg body weight, 30-60 min pre-session; keep under 9 mg/kg
A-strong.notes: Coffee counts. Delaying first caffeine 90-120 min after waking is a Huberman protocol with limited direct trials. Cut off 8-10 h before sleep. For a 75 kg person 3-6 mg/kg is 225-450 mg.

A-strong.name: Sports drink / gels (carbohydrate)
A-strong.dose: 30-60 g/h for 1-2.5 h sessions; up to 90 g/h for over 2.5 h (glucose:fructose mix)

B-good.name: Sodium bicarbonate
B-good.notes: GI distress is common and can cancel the benefit. Trial in training first.

B-good.name: Beta-alanine
B-good.notes: Harmless tingling. Little benefit for steady endurance.

B-good.name: Dietary nitrate (beet juice)
B-good.dose: about 6-8 mmol (roughly 400-500 mg) nitrate 2-3 h pre-event
B-good.notes: Effect is smaller in highly trained athletes.

B-good.name: Whey or other protein powder
B-good.dose: 20-40 g per feeding, 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day total protein for exercisers
B-good.goal: convenience protein to hit daily targets
B-good.notes: A food, not a performance drug. Only worth it if cheaper per gram than eggs or chicken; it is not.
sources: ISSN protein and exercise position stand (Springer 10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8)

C-situational.name: Vitamin D3
C-situational.notes: Huberman Wiki cites 2,000-4,000 IU. Blood-test rather than guess.

C-situational.name: Fish oil (EPA+DHA)
C-situational.dose: 1-3 g EPA+DHA/day if you rarely eat fish
C-situational.notes: Skip if you eat oily fish 2x/week.

C-situational.name: Magnesium glycinate
C-situational.goal: sleep, cramps if intake is low
C-situational.notes: Modest evidence; diet (oats, beans, rice) already provides some.

C-situational.name: Sodium / electrolyte mix
C-situational.dose: 300-700 mg sodium per hour in hot or long sessions
C-situational.goal: prevent hyponatremia and cramping in long endurance
C-situational.notes: Only needed for sessions over about 60-90 min or heavy sweating.

D-weak-or-skip.name: NMN / NR
D-weak-or-skip.notes: Human performance evidence is thin; expensive.

D-weak-or-skip.name: BPC-157
D-weak-or-skip.notes: Not approved, minimal human data, and banned in tested sport (WADA). Do not use.

D-weak-or-skip.name: Ashwagandha
D-weak-or-skip.notes: Some small stress trials; quality control is poor; drug interactions exist.

D-weak-or-skip.name: BCAAs
D-weak-or-skip.notes: Redundant if total protein is adequate.

budgetStack: Creatine (3-5 g) + coffee + cheap real food covers the high-evidence tier for under $15/month. Add vitamin D only after a blood test.
